title: Give me truth
hook: rather than love, money, fame, give me truth (Walden 18)
tomorrow: the sun is a morning star

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one who falls behind on the trail, and Thoreau's generous perhaps. Your line was a different drummer.

Love. Money. Fame. Set them on a table in front of a stranger, ask them to pick one, and you'd learn a lot about the stranger. A love song picks the first. A business plan, the second. A talent show, the third. A few pages from the end of Walden, Thoreau pushes all three aside and asks for something that doesn't fit on the table at all. It's one short sentence, and it puts love on the losing side.
screen: `LOVE. MONEY. FAME.` → `PICK ONE.` → `THOREAU PUSHES ALL THREE AWAY.`

segments.voice: The sentence, from Walden's Conclusion: "Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth." First, the shock of the list. Money and fame are easy to set aside in a book about a cabin. But love? He doesn't say love is bad. He says that if he had to choose, he'd take truth first, maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love. Second, a dinner. Right after the line, he tells of a table with rich food, plenty of wine and attentive service, where sincerity and truth were missing. He went away hungry. A full plate, and he left hungry. That's how he measures a meal: not by what was served, but by whether anyone was honest at it. Third, what truth means to him here. A little earlier in the chapter he writes, "Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe." For Thoreau, truth isn't mainly a fact you look up. It's the difference between a real life and a performed one. Fourth, the cost. Choosing truth over love, money and fame means some rooms get colder, and some tables you leave early. Thoreau seems to accept that. He'd rather go home hungry than stay full on make-believe. Readers are free to argue with him, but the line is plain about where he stood.
screen: `TRUTH OVER LOVE, MONEY, FAME.` · `A RICH TABLE, AND HE LEFT HUNGRY.` · `SAY WHAT YOU HAVE TO SAY.` · then, large: `ANY TRUTH IS BETTER THAN MAKE-BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: Let one place come to mind where you say what you ought instead of what you have to say: a meeting, a family dinner, a friendship where something has gone unsaid. Don't rehearse a speech; just find the one true sentence underneath, short and kind, and say it silently a few times. Notice how it sits.
Give me truth. Thoreau's choice, ahead of love, money and fame, and his reason for leaving a rich table hungry. Today's word.
Your line: give me truth. A full plate is no meal if nobody at the table is honest. That's day one thousand two hundred forty-three.

screen: `DAY 1243 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SUN IS A MORNING STAR.`

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often hold this line up as Thoreau's case for sincerity: saying what is actually so, even when the expected answer would be more comfortable.

notes: Confirm exact wording against the 1854 text: 'Rather than love, than money, than fame, give me truth.' and 'Say what you have to say, not what you ought. Any truth is better than make-believe.'
Paraphrased, confirm: 'I sat at a table where were rich food and wine in abundance, and obsequious attendance, but sincerity and truth were not; and I went away hungry from the inhospitable board.'
'Maybe because love built on a pretense isn't quite love' is offered as an interpretation, hedged; a reviewer may cut it.
'Readers are free to argue with him' is the writer's framing, not a claim about reception.
